chapter.title: Start walking without stumbling

cards.body:
Picture a good walk leader at the gate. She doesn't shuffle off while people are still tying laces, mumbling "so, um, I guess we'll head... that way?" She stops, waits until every face is turned to her, points, and says: "We're going to the old mill. It's 40 minutes. Follow me."

**Your first 20 seconds are the gate.** Stop, wait, then say the one sentence that names where you're all going.
cards.simpler:
Think of a good walk leader at the gate. She doesn't wander off while people are still tying their shoes, muttering about which way to go. She stops. She waits until everyone is looking at her. Then she points and says: "We're going to the old mill. It's 40 minutes. Follow me."

**Your first 20 seconds are the gate.** Stop, wait, then say the one sentence that tells everyone where you're all going.

cards.prompt: Maya stands up to tell 6 teammates about a new shift rota. Which opening is the walk leader at the gate?

options.text: "Um, hi, can everyone hear me? OK so I'm going to talk a bit about, um, the rota thing."
Two seconds of silence, feet still, then: "By Friday, every shift on this team will have a backup person."
"Before I start, sorry, I'm really not great at this, so bear with me."

whyNot.a: That's tying your laces in front of everyone, not pointing at the mill: the sound check and the "um" tell the group you haven't decided where you're going yet.
whyNot.c: That's apologising for the walk before it starts: it names your nerves, not the destination, so the group looks at you instead of the route.

cards.reteach: The opening has one job: tell people where they're going. Silence first, then a sentence with the destination in it. Anything else, a sound check, an apology, a warm-up, delays the pointing finger and makes the group wonder if there is a destination at all.

cards.title: One sentence, from memory, after a pause
cards.body:
You memorise exactly one sentence of your talk, word for word: the first one. It's the destination sentence from chapter 1, or a shorter cousin of it. Everything after can come from your card. The first sentence comes from your head, because your eyes need to be on the room, not on paper.

**Before you say it, stop and count 2 in your head.** This pause is the hardest part. To you it feels like a hole. To the people watching it looks like someone who knows where the mill is.

The pause does a second job: it lets the room's noise die down, so your sentence lands on quiet.
cards.simpler:
Learn exactly one sentence of your talk by heart: the first one. It's the sentence from chapter 1 that says where you're taking people, or a shorter version of it. The rest can come from your card. The first sentence comes from your head, so your eyes can be on the room, not on paper.

**Before you say it, stop and count 2 in your head.** This pause feels like a hole to you. To the people watching, it looks like someone who knows the way. It also lets the room go quiet, so your sentence lands on silence.

cards.title: Dev and the 9:15 standup
cards.body:
Dev, a junior on a team of 7, had 3 minutes at a Tuesday meeting to move the daily standup 15 minutes later. He reached the end of the table, stopped, and counted *one, two* while looking at Sana, the person nearest him. Then: "If we move standup to 9:15, we get 20 more minutes of actual work every morning."

Someone put down their coffee. That was the whole pause: 2 seconds. Afterwards Sana told him, "You seemed very sure." He had been sure of exactly one sentence. It was enough to start.
cards.simpler:
Dev was a junior on a team of 7. He had 3 minutes at a Tuesday meeting to ask for the daily standup to move 15 minutes later. He walked to the end of the table, stopped, and counted *one, two* while looking at Sana, the person closest to him. Then he said: "If we move standup to 9:15, we get 20 more minutes of real work every morning."

Someone set down their coffee. That was the whole pause. Afterwards Sana said, "You seemed very sure." He had been sure of one sentence. That was enough.

cards.prompt: You're planning your own first 20 seconds for Thursday. Which plan applies the chapter?

options.text: Start speaking while still walking to the front, so there's never an awkward silence.
Reach your spot, stop, count 2, then say the first sentence from memory while looking at one person.
Reach your spot, stop, then read the first sentence off your card so you get the words exactly right.

whyNot.a: That's filling the silence, not using it: speaking while you move means your sentence arrives before you do, and nobody hears it.
whyNot.c: That's the plan for the rest of the talk, not the opening: the card is fine later, but the first sentence is the one you memorise so your eyes are on the room, not on paper.

cards.reteach: Three things happen in order: arrive, pause, speak. The pause is on purpose, 2 counts. The first sentence is the one bit you know by heart, so you can look at a person while you say it. Reading it or saying it on the move both break that eye contact.

cards.title: What your feet and hands do
cards.body:
Nerves go to your legs first. They want to sway, shift, or step backwards. So before the pause, **plant both feet flat, about shoulder width, and leave them there** for the whole first sentence. Still feet read as calm even when nothing inside you is.

Hands: let them hang at your sides, or hold your card at waist height in one hand. Not in pockets, not clasped in front like a goalkeeper waiting for a penalty. Hands at your sides feel strange to you and look completely normal to everyone else.

Eyes: pick one friendly face and say the whole first sentence to them. One person, one sentence. Then you can look around.
cards.simpler:
Nerves hit your legs first. They want to sway, shift, or step back. So before the pause, **plant both feet flat, about shoulder width, and leave them there** for the whole first sentence. Still feet look calm, even when you don't feel calm.

Let your hands hang at your sides, or hold your card at waist height in one hand. Not in pockets. Not clasped in front like a goalkeeper waiting for a penalty kick. Hands at your sides feel odd to you and look normal to everyone else.

Pick one friendly face and say the whole first sentence to that person. Then look around.

cards.body:
Priya had her first sentence memorised perfectly. But she started saying it from her chair, kept saying it while she walked to the front, and arrived at her spot having already finished it. Eight people heard the second half of a sentence delivered to the side of her head.

**If your mouth is moving while your feet are moving, you've started too early.** Spot it in rehearsal: the first word should come out after your feet have been still for 2 counts.
cards.simpler:
Priya knew her first sentence perfectly. But she started saying it from her chair, kept talking while she walked to the front, and had finished it by the time she arrived. Eight people heard the second half of a sentence spoken to the side of her head.

**If your mouth is moving while your feet are moving, you've started too early.** Catch it when you practise. The first word should come out only after your feet have been still for 2 counts.

cards.prompt: Your first 20 seconds have 3 parts. Which list has them in the right order?

options.text: Say the sentence, then pause, then plant your feet.
Plant your feet, pause for 2 counts, then say the sentence to one person.
Pause for 2 counts, say the sentence, then plant your feet.

whyNot.a: That's Priya's order: the sentence arrives before you do, and the pause lands after the only words you memorised.
whyNot.c: That's pausing while still unsettled: your feet are the first thing to go still, because the pause only looks calm if you aren't swaying through it.

cards.reteach: Think of the gate. First you stop at it: feet planted. Then you wait for the faces to turn: 2 counts of silence. Then you point: the one sentence, said to one person. Stop, wait, point. The order never changes.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Reach your spot, plant your feet, count 2 in silence, then say the one sentence you know by heart, the one that names where you're taking them, to one person's face. **Don't start speaking until you've stopped moving.**
cards.simpler: Here is the whole thing in one breath. Walk to your spot. Plant your feet. Count 2 in silence. Then say the one sentence you know by heart, the one that tells people where you're taking them, to one person's face. **Don't start speaking until you've stopped moving.** That is the order every time: feet first, pause second, words last.

cards.body: Tonight, in your kitchen: walk to a spot, stop, plant both feet, count 2, then say your chapter 1 sentence out loud to the kettle. Hands at your sides. Do it 3 times.
cards.simpler: Tonight, in your kitchen, try this. Walk to a spot and stop. Plant both feet flat. Count 2 in your head. Then say your chapter 1 sentence out loud to the kettle. Keep your hands at your sides. Do the whole thing 3 times. It will feel silly, and that's fine. **Practise the stop and the pause** until your feet are still before your first word.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open a talk from memory with a sentence that names the destination, standing still, after a 2-second pause.
